x_patch2vuln.patchSummary: In note_variables.py, a new _audience_can_view() function verifies that the destination case's organisations are a subset of the referenced case's organisations before resolving cross-case or cross-task references; case_notes.py passes the resolved case object instead of a raw integer ID. In chatbot_core.py, a _chatbot_api_request() validator and a _READ_API_PATHS regex allow-list are added; unsupported methods, external URLs, path traversal, admin routes, and non-allow-listed operations are refused before the MCP call. descriptions.value: HotGo 2.18.6 through 2.19.0 contains an information disclosure vulnerability that allows authenticated backend users to read other administrators' private letters because the messageIds helper omits the receiver filter. Low-privilege users can call GET /admin/notice/pullMessages, which is exempt from role permission checks via exceptAuth, to retrieve titles, contents and senders of private letters.

In Dolibarr before 24.0.3, dolForgeSQLCriteriaCallback() in htdocs/core/lib/functions.lib.php allows account takeover because it strips only a single table-name prefix from a Universal Search Filter (sqlfilters) operand before checking it against the forbidden-field denylist (pass, pass_crypted, api_key). MariaDB and MySQL accept a two-level qualification such as schema.alias.column, so an operand of the form dolibarr.u.pass_crypted survives the check and is emitted into the WHERE clause. A remote authenticated user holding only the holiday read and readall permissions, which confer no user-management or administrative access, can use the resulting boolean oracle at GET /api/index.php/holidays to recover any user's bcrypt password hash and api_key one character at a time, including an administrator's. Because api_key is accepted directly by the REST API as a bearer credential, this yields full administrative control of the application. This bypasses the fix for CVE-2026-89012, which added only a strtolower() call and did not address prefix depth. The same denylist also omits pass_temp, which stores a password in cleartext, as well as national_registration_number, salary, birth, address, personal_mobile and note_private.

descriptions.description: CWE-424 Improper Protection of Alternate Path

descriptions.value:
FlowIntel contains an authorization bypass in its case serialization logic that allows an authenticated user to view metadata of private cases they do not have access to.

When a case is linked to another case, the JSON representation of the source case included the ID, title, and description of every linked case regardless of the requesting user's permissions. This affected multiple access paths:

- Browser views (case detail, case info, search, calendar)
- REST API endpoints (get case, list cases, search, title lookup, completed/not-completed lists)
- Internal tooling and connector module context building

An attacker with valid credentials and access to any case that contains a link to a private case could enumerate the private case's identifier, title, and description without holding a membership or role on that private case. The exposure occurred because the serialization method did not receive or evaluate the acting user's identity before including linked-case data in the response.

Security impact:
- Disclosure of private case identifiers, titles, and descriptions to unauthorized users
- Facilitation of further targeted attacks against the exposed private cases
- Bypass of the intended per-case access control model

Affected versions: FlowIntel prior to 4.1.0
CAPEC-12 Application Metadata Discovery

descriptions.description: CWE-200 Exposure of Sensitive Information to an Unauthorized Actor

solutions.value: The serialization method now accepts the acting user as a parameter and filters linked cases based on the user's authorization. When an authenticated user is provided, only linked cases the user is permitted to view are included. When no user is provided (internal or anonymous callers), the method fails closed by excluding all private linked cases. All call sites across browser views, API endpoints, calendar, search, tools, and internal core operations were updated to pass the resolved user identity, ensuring consistent enforcement regardless of the access path.

cna.title: Validation bypass of extra data keys in JSON model validation

descriptions.value:
When validating JSON data into a model allowing extra data, the keys of extra data aren't validated against the key type annotated on __pydantic_extra__, resulting in extra data not matching the declared type. This is the case if you define __pydantic_extra__ as e.g. dict[Annotated[str, Field(pattern=r'^x_')], int].

The validate_json_by_iteration() method (in pydantic-core/src/validators/model_fields.rs), used to validate JSON data into models, only validates the values of extra data, and stores the keys as is.

The issue was fixed in commit 4c65dbda9970a488e2ff21c8693fc6f6d70a3358.

Impact: validation bypass, as extra data returned by validation doesn't match the declared type. supportingMedia.value:
Summary

When validating JSON data into a model allowing extra data, the keys of extra data aren't validated against the key type annotated on __pydantic_extra__, resulting in extra data not matching the declared type. This is the case if you define __pydantic_extra__ as e.g. dict[Annotated[str, Field(pattern=r'^x_')], int].

Details

The validate_json_by_iteration() method (in pydantic-core/src/validators/model_fields.rs), used to validate JSON data into models, only validates the values of extra data, and stores the keys as is (L605-L623):

ExtraBehavior::Allow => {
    // the key is stored as is, without being validated:
    let py_key: Bound<'_, PyString> = new_py_string(py, key, state.cache_str());
    if let Some(validator) = &self.extras_validator {
        match validator.validate(py, value, state) {
            Ok(value) => {
                model_extra_dict.set_item(&py_key, value)?;
                fields_set.add(py_key)?;
            }
            // ...
        }
    }
    // ...
}

Python mode validation isn't affected.

The issue was fixed in commit 4c65dbda9970a488e2ff21c8693fc6f6d70a3358.

Impact

Validation bypass: extra data returned by validation doesn't match the declared type. Affected are applications validating untrusted JSON data into models allowing extra data (with extra='allow'), with a key type annotated on __pydantic_extra__ (e.g. dict[Annotated[str, Field(pattern=...)], int]), using Pydantic from 2.13.0 up to (but excluding) 2.14.2.

Python mode validation isn't affected.

x_patch2vuln.subject: fix: [security] Pulls and feeds no longer update sharing
x_patch2vuln.fixSummary: The fix introduces a proper authorization check for remote capture operations. The captureRemote method now receives the full server context (or null for feeds) and stores both the internal flag and the remote organization identifier. A new __remoteMayUpdate method verifies that, for non-internal pulls, the remote organization is a member of the target sharing group (as owning org, in the SharingGroupOrg list, or via an all_orgs entry). For feeds (server is null), the update is always refused. When the check fails, the sharing group record is left unchanged while the pulled data still attaches to it, preserving data integrity without granting unauthorized metadata modification.
assumptions: The affected MISP version range is not specified in the patch; all versions prior to this commit are assumed affected.
The PR:L assumption assumes the attacker must be an authenticated user with sync or feed privileges; the patch does not explicitly state the minimum role required.
SI:N assumes that modifying a local sharing group's metadata does not propagate integrity changes to remote MISP instances; the patch does not provide evidence of cross-instance impact.
The CAPEC-114 mapping is the closest available pattern; no CAPEC precisely describes a missing membership-authorization check on a shared resource update.
The patch commit date is 2026-11-12; the actual release timeline and fixed version are unknown.
The Co-Authored-By line credits 'Claude Opus 5.5' as a remediation developer; this is recorded as-is from the commit metadata without independent verification.
x_patch2vuln.patchSummary: Three files are modified. In Feed.php, two calls to SharingGroup::captureRemote change the first argument from false to null, indicating a feed has no server context. In Server.php, the pull method now passes the full $server array instead of a derived boolean. In SharingGroup.php, the static $remoteCapture variable changes from a boolean to an associative array holding internal (bool) and remote_org_id (int|null). The captureRemote method signature changes from accepting a bool to accepting an array or null. A new private method __remoteMayUpdate is added, which returns true for internal links, and for non-internal links checks that remote_org_id is set, the group is not local, and the remote org matches the group's org_id, appears in SharingGroupOrg, or is covered by an all_orgs SharingGroupServer entry. In captureSGExisting, a guard clause is inserted before the existing update logic: if a remote capture is active and __remoteMayUpdate returns false, the method returns the existing group id without further
x_patch2vuln.cvssRationale: AV:N: MISP is a network-accessible web application; pulls and feeds are initiated over HTTP. AC:L: An attacker with a configured pull or feed simply triggers the operation; no race conditions or special timing are needed. AT:N: No manipulation of the attack target is required. PR:L: The attacker must be an authenticated user with sync or feed privileges to initiate a pull or feed. UI:N: No victim interaction is required; the operation runs server-side. VC:N: No confidentiality impact is evident from the patch. VI:L: The integrity impact is limited to sharing group metadata (local flag, modified timestamp, org associations) being altered by an unauthorized remote entity. VA:N: No availability impact. SC:N/SI:N/SA:N: No evidence of impact on other systems; the modification is confined to the local MISP instance's sharing group record. SI is set to N rather than L because the patch does not demonstrate that the metadata change propagates to or alters the behavior of connected MISP instances; this is an assumption recorded below.

capecRationale.rationale: The remote sync user or feed process is granted the ability to modify sharing group metadata beyond what its organizational membership should permit. The authorization logic incorrectly treats any non-internal remote capture as having the same update rights as an internal one, or fails to distinguish between a remote entity that is a group member and one that is not. This is the closest CAPEC pattern to an authorization-logic flaw where the privilege boundary is miscalculated. Uncertainty: no CAPEC pattern precisely describes 'missing membership check on a shared resource update'; CAPEC-114 is selected as the best available match for an incorrectly scoped privilege.

weaknessRationale.rationale: The application failed to verify that the remote server's organization was a member of the target sharing group before permitting metadata updates during pull and feed operations. The authorization check was simply absent for the non-internal remote case; only a boolean internal flag was stored and checked, with no membership validation.

solutions.value: The fix introduces a proper authorization check for remote capture operations. The captureRemote method now receives the full server context (or null for feeds) and stores both the internal flag and the remote organization identifier. A new __remoteMayUpdate method verifies that, for non-internal pulls, the remote organization is a member of the target sharing group (as owning org, in the SharingGroupOrg list, or via an all_orgs entry). For feeds (server is null), the update is always refused. descriptions.value: MISP contains an authorization flaw in the handling of remote pull and feed operations. When a non-internal pull or a feed processes incoming data and encounters an existing sharing group, the application did not verify that the remote server's organization was actually a member of that sharing group before allowing the group's metadata to be updated. The captureRemote mechanism previously stored only a boolean flag indicating whether the link was internal, and the authorization check in captureSGExisting relied solely on that flag. For non-internal pulls and feeds, the check was insufficient: a remote server whose organization was not a member of the target sharing group could still cause the group record to be modified (for example, altering the local flag, the modified timestamp, or other group properties). A feed, which has no associated server organization at all, could likewise trigger an update to an existing sharing group's metadata. The security impact is an integrity violation: an authenticated remote entity with sync or feed privileges can alter sharing group attributes that govern how data is distributed among organizations, potentially changing the local flag or other access-relevant properties of groups it does not belong to. The vulnerability requires an authenticated user with the ability to initiate a pull or feed (a sync user or feed administrator) and a target sharing group that exists on the local instance. No unauthenticated access or user interaction is required.

flowintel contains a log injection vulnerability in its case history (audit log) subsystem. The case history is stored as a line-delimited file where each line represents a single event attributed to a specific user. User-controlled fields, including user names, event messages, and case titles used during case merging, were written to the history file without sanitizing embedded line separator characters (such as carriage return, line feed, vertical tab, form feed, and Unicode line/paragraph separators).

An authenticated user with the ability to create or modify case history entries could embed line separators in these fields. Upon writing, the injected separators would split a single intended entry into multiple lines, each of which the history format interprets as a distinct event. This allows an attacker to forge additional history entries attributed to arbitrary users, corrupting the audit trail and undermining the integrity of case records.

The vulnerability affects the case history append and merge operations. No authentication bypass or privilege escalation is required beyond normal case-management access.

Affected versions: flowintel prior to 4.1.0.
CAPEC-66 HTTP Request/Response Splitting

descriptions.description: CWE-117 Improper Output Neutralization for Logs

solutions.value: The fix introduces a sanitization helper that replaces all splitlines()-recognized line separator characters (CR, LF, VT, FF, file/group/record separators, NEL, Unicode line and paragraph separators) with a single space before any user-authored content is written to the case history file. The helper is applied to the author name, the event message, and the case title during merge operations, ensuring each history entry remains on exactly one line and cannot be split into forged entries.

descriptions.value:
flowintel contains a vulnerability in the MISP correlation feature that allows unauthorized disclosure of case identifiers.

The application failed to enforce proper access controls when generating correlation lists for MISP attributes. Specifically, the system did not verify whether the requesting user had permission to view the source case or the matching cases returned in the correlation results. This lack of authorization checks allowed authenticated users to potentially discover the existence of cases they do not have access to, leading to information disclosure.

The vulnerability affects the following components:
- Case correlation logic
- API endpoints for retrieving correlation attributes
- MISP object handling

Affected versions: < 4.1.0
CAPEC-126 Forced Browsing

descriptions.description: CWE-639 Authorization Bypass Through User-Controlled Key

solutions.value: The vulnerability is remediated by enforcing strict access control checks on both the source case and the resulting correlation list. The system now verifies that the acting user has permission to view the source case before processing correlations. Additionally, the resulting list of matching case IDs is filtered to include only cases that the user is authorized to access. This ensures that no unauthorized case identifiers are disclosed to the user.

descriptions.value:
flowintel contains an Insecure Direct Object Reference (IDOR) vulnerability affecting multiple endpoints that manage child records of cases and tasks. An authenticated user with access to one case or task could read or modify records belonging to other cases by supplying identifiers of those records directly in the request.

Affected operations include:
- Reading task notes, subtasks, and URL tools by referencing their IDs without verifying they belong to the authorized task
- Retrieving task assignees for a task belonging to a different case
- Editing or deleting timeline events and timeline event links belonging to another case
- Editing or removing case connectors belonging to another case
- Invoking connector module operations (MISP, generic connectors, worker calls) by combining an authorized case with a connector link from a different case

The root cause is that the application authorized the parent resource (case or task) in the URL but then fetched or operated on the child record independently without verifying the child's ownership relationship to the authorized parent.

Security impact: an authenticated user can exfiltrate sensitive threat intelligence data from cases they do not have access to, and can modify or delete timeline entries, connector configurations, and other records in unauthorized cases, leading to data integrity loss and potential disruption of incident response workflows.

Affected versions: flowintel prior to 4.1.0
CAPEC-1 Tamper with URLs

descriptions.description: CWE-639 Authorization Bypass Through User-Controlled Key

solutions.value: The fix enforces ownership validation by requiring the authorized parent case or task ID in every core method that reads or writes child records. Before returning data or performing writes, each child record's case_id or task_id is explicitly compared against the resolved parent. Mismatched records are rejected with a 404 or 403 response. Connector module context building now verifies connector-to-case ownership before preparing module data, resolving credentials, or executing sync operations. Instance visibility checks are applied consistently across both web and API routes.

CAPEC-1 (Tamper with URLs) is the closest available pattern; the actual attack is parameter substitution in REST endpoints rather than classic URL tampering, but no more specific CAPEC exists for IDOR via REST identifiers.
VC:H and VI:H assume the data in other cases is sensitive and that modification/deletion constitutes full integrity loss; the patch does not specify data classification.
The patch does not indicate whether the vulnerability was disclosed publicly or under embargo; exploitation status is assumed to be 'none' based on absence of evidence.

The application did not validate that the referenced object belonged to the authorized parent, allowing cross-tenant data access. cna.title: Org.keycloak:keycloak-services: pre-revocation id tokens can mint fresh uma rpts after realm not-before

descriptions.value: A flaw was found in Keycloak. When an administrator revokes tokens by setting a not-before revocation cutoff, Keycloak fails to enforce this boundary when processing User-Managed Access (UMA) grant requests using ID token claims. An authenticated remote user with an active session can submit a previously revoked ID token to receive a fresh Requesting Party Token (RPT). This flaw allows an attacker to bypass token revocation and retain unauthorized access to protected resources.

descriptions.description: Use of a Key Past its Expiration Date

cna.x_redhatCweChain: CWE-324: Use of a Key Past its Expiration Date

workarounds.value:
Explicitly terminate active user sessions when revoking tokens, or disable User-Managed Access (UMA) authorization on clients where fine-grained authorization is not needed.

To reduce exposure:
- In the Keycloak Administration Console, navigate to the target realm, select 'Sessions', and explicitly terminate active sessions for the relevant user or realm rather than relying solely on the not-before timestamp cutoff.
- For OpenID Connect clients that do not require fine-grained resource permissions, ensure that 'Authorization Enabled' is set to 'OFF' in the client settings.

Caveats:
Terminating active user sessions will immediately disconnect active sessions and require users to re-authenticate. Disabling authorization services on a client disables the issuance of Requesting Party Tokens (RPTs) for that client. These configuration changes take effect immediately and do not require restarting the Keycloak service.

cna.title: Unbounded exponent in Fraction validation

descriptions.value:
Validating an untrusted string in exponent notation into a Fraction field computes the full power of ten without any bound: an input of a few bytes takes seconds to validate.

String inputs are passed to the Fraction constructor. For strings in exponent notation (e.g. '1e8000000'), CPython computes the corresponding power of ten as an integer (in Lib/fractions.py).

The issue was fixed in commit 69ed168e9ad465eef4c8d81efb152a93b604daf5. For strings in exponent notation, the exponent is now parsed before calling the Fraction constructor, and exponents larger than 4300 (in absolute value) are rejected.

Impact: denial of service through validation of untrusted input. Affected are applications validating untrusted strings into Fraction fields (in both JSON and Python mode, including in strict mode), using Pydantic from 2.10.0 up to (but excluding) 2.14.0.

From 2.14.0, exponents larger than 4300 (in absolute value) are rejected, matching the maximum number of digits accepted for integers.

supportingMedia.value:
Summary

Validating an untrusted string in exponent notation into a Fraction field computes the full power of ten without any bound: an input of a few bytes takes seconds to validate.

Details

String inputs are passed to the Fraction constructor. For strings in exponent notation (e.g. '1e8000000'), CPython computes the corresponding power of ten as an integer (Lib/fractions.py):

exp = m.group('exp')
if exp:
    exp = int(exp)
    if exp >= 0:
        numerator *= 10**exp
    else:
        denominator *= 10**-exp

The issue was fixed in commit 69ed168e9ad465eef4c8d81efb152a93b604daf5. For strings in exponent notation, the exponent is now parsed before calling the Fraction constructor, and exponents larger than 4300 (in absolute value) are rejected.

Impact

Denial of service through validation of untrusted input. Affected are applications validating untrusted strings into Fraction fields (in both JSON and Python mode, including in strict mode), using Pydantic from 2.10.0 up to (but excluding) 2.14.0.

From 2.14.0, exponents larger than 4300 (in absolute value) are rejected, matching the maximum number of digits accepted for integers.

cna.title: Tool result data shaped like a file is rebuilt as a file download or provider file reference when message history is reloaded

descriptions.value: When message history is serialized and loaded again, a tool result that contains a JSON object in the serialized shape of one of Pydantic AI's file types is rebuilt as that file. A third party who controls data a tool returns, such as a record that an MCP server or a function tool returns from an external system, can use this to make the application download a URL on its local network, or make the model provider read an s3:// object or uploaded file with the application's credentials. Applications are affected when tool results can contain third-party data, message history containing those results is serialized and loaded again (stored history, history a UI adapter holds on the server, or Temporal, DBOS or Prefect durable execution), and the model is one Pydantic AI downloads files for, one that honors force_download, or one whose provider resolves non-HTTP file URLs or uploaded files. History that a client submits through the Vercel AI or AG-UI adapter in the default mode is not affected. The issue is fixed in pydantic-ai and pydantic-ai-slim 1.107.10 and 2.66.0.

descriptions.description: CWE-843: Access of Resource Using Incompatible Type

descriptions.value:
flowintel contains multiple related flaws that allow an authenticated attacker to inject arbitrary HTML or script into pages viewed by other users.

- Timeline rendering: the timeline library's autolinking feature rewrote already-sanitised case notes and imported MISP attribute values into generated HTML link elements. Crafted text containing quote characters could break out of the generated attribute context, altering the surrounding markup and enabling script execution in the victim's browser.

- Search highlighting: the highlight injection logic used a regular expression to locate text between angle brackets and spliced <mark> elements into the resulting string. Because the pattern could match inside HTML attribute values, the rewrite could corrupt or inject content into attributes of already-sanitised markup, again leading to DOM-based cross-site scripting.

- Content-Type confusion: three analyser selection endpoints returned session-stored JSON strings with a text/html content type. A browser receiving such a response will parse and render the body as HTML, so any HTML or script embedded in the stored value is executed in the victim's context.

Preconditions: the attacker must be an authenticated user with the ability to create or import case content (notes, MISP attributes) containing specially crafted quote or angle-bracket sequences. The victim must subsequently open the affected case timeline, run a search, or request one of the selection endpoints.

Impact: successful exploitation yields DOM-based cross-site scripting in the victim's browser session, potentially allowing disclosure of case data, session manipulation, or execution of arbitrary actions under the victim's identity.

Affected versions: flowintel prior to 4.1.0.
CAPEC-6 DOM Based XSS
CAPEC-1 XSS - Reflected

descriptions.description: CWE-79 Improper Neutralization of Input in Web Page ('Cross-site Scripting')
CWE-799 Improper Control of Resources Identifiers

solutions.value: The vulnerability is remediated by eliminating the three injection paths: (1) autolinking is disabled on every timeline event so the library no longer rewrites sanitised HTML; (2) search and auto-highlight marks are now created by walking the DOM text nodes and setting textContent, which cannot alter existing attributes or split character entities; (3) the three selection endpoints now decode the stored JSON once, respond with application/json and X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff, and reject malformed or excessively nested payloads with a 400 JSON error, preventing the browser from interpreting the body as HTML.

cna.title: flowintel DOM-based XSS via Timeline Autolinking, Search Highlighting, and Content-Type Confusion

ai_annotations.description: Draft vulnerability metadata was generated from a git-format patch using an Ollama-hosted language model. Human validation is required before publication.

assumptions: The affected_version field in the metadata is recorded as '0', which is treated as a placeholder meaning all versions prior to 4.1.0 are affected; no earlier version boundary is specified.
The CVSS PR:L assumes the attacker needs an authenticated account to create the malicious case content; if unauthenticated import paths exist, PR could be N.
The CVSS UI:A assumes the victim must navigate to the affected page; if the malicious content is auto-loaded in a dashboard or notification, UI could be N.
CAPEC-1 (Reflected XSS) is included as a secondary mapping for the content-type confusion path; the primary and more certain mapping is CAPEC-6 (DOM Based XSS).
The nested-JSON rejection (RecursionError guard) suggests a potential DoS vector via deeply nested JSON, but no separate DoS impact is scored because the primary vulnerability is XSS.
No public exploit or PoC is referenced; exploitation status is assumed to be 'none'.

capecRationale.rationale: The primary exploitation path is client-side: attacker-controlled text (case notes, MISP values, search terms) is processed by JavaScript in the browser (TimelineJS autolinking, regex-based highlight injection) and the resulting DOM manipulation injects executable markup. The content-type confusion endpoint is a secondary vector but the dominant pattern is DOM-based script injection. CAPEC-6 is the closest standard attack pattern; the mapping is confident because the patch explicitly addresses client-side HTML rewriting of user-supplied content.

The three selection endpoints that returned session JSON as text/html could be leveraged as a reflected XSS vector if the session content is influenced by a prior request parameter. This is a secondary, less certain mapping; CAPEC-6 remains the primary pattern. Included because the content-type confusion path is a distinct mechanism from pure DOM manipulation.

x_patch2vuln.cvssRationale: AV:N – the application is a web service reachable over the network. AC:L – crafting quote-bearing text in case notes or MISP attributes is straightforward; no race or special timing is needed. AT:N – no active attack or prior compromise is required beyond normal authenticated use. PR:L – the attacker needs an authenticated account to create or import the malicious content (endpoints are login_required). UI:A – the victim must actively open the case timeline, run a search, or request a selection endpoint for the injected markup to execute. VC:L – XSS can expose case data, session tokens, or other sensitive information visible in the browser. VI:L – the attacker can modify displayed content or trigger actions in the victim's session. VA:N – no evidence of denial-of-service impact beyond the nested-JSON guard. SC:N – no cross-component or cross-origin impact is demonstrated. SI:L – other authenticated users viewing the same case could be affected by the stored malicious content. SA:N – no elevation of security authority is indicated.
x_patch2vuln.fixSummary: The vulnerability is remediated by eliminating the three injection paths: (1) autolinking is disabled on every timeline event so the library no longer rewrites sanitised HTML; (2) search and auto-highlight marks are now created by walking the DOM text nodes and setting textContent, which cannot alter existing attributes or split character entities; (3) the three selection endpoints now decode the stored JSON once, respond with application/json and X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff, and reject malformed or excessively nested payloads with a 400 JSON error, preventing the browser from interpreting the body as HTML.

x_patch2vuln.patchSummary: In case_history.js and timeline_view.js, an autolink: false property is added to each TimelineJS event object to suppress linkification. In smart-render.js, the previous regex-based string replacement (html.replace(/>([^<]*)</g, ...)) is replaced with a DOM TreeWalker that iterates text nodes, builds <mark> elements via document.createElement and textContent, and splices them into a DocumentFragment, preserving all existing attributes and entities. A new count_html_matches helper counts matches across text nodes. The plain-text fallback branches that performed raw regex replacement on escaped strings are removed. In misp_modules.py, a new _selected_json_response helper decodes the session value with json.loads, wraps it in jsonify, sets X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff, and returns a 400 JSON error on TypeError, ValueError, or RecursionError. The three get_*_selected endpoints are updated to call this helper instead of returning the raw session string.

The content-type confusion (serving application/json data as text/html) is a secondary weakness that amplifies the XSS by causing the browser to parse the response body as HTML. This is a narrower, supporting CWE.

descriptions.value:
FlowIntel contains a resource exhaustion vulnerability in its file-to-note conversion feature. When a user converts an attached CSV or JSON file into a case note, the application renders the data as a Markdown table by padding every row to the maximum column count. A crafted file with a small number of filled cells but a very large number of columns (or keys) causes the application to allocate a quadratic number of padded table cells, potentially exhausting a worker process in memory or CPU.

The same issue affects nested JSON values rendered inside table cells, where pretty-printed indentation further inflates the output size.

Preconditions:
- An authenticated user with access to a case in FlowIntel
- Ability to attach and convert a CSV or JSON file to a note

Impact:
- Denial of service: exhaustion of a worker process, potentially disrupting service for other users
- No confidentiality or integrity impact

Affected versions: FlowIntel prior to 4.1.0
CAPEC-10 Application Resource Exhaustion
CAPEC-124 Resource Exhaustion via Algorithmic Complexity

descriptions.description: CWE-770 Allocation of Resources Without Limits or Throttling

solutions.value: The fix introduces bounds on table expansion: a maximum padded-cell count (50,000) and a maximum padding ratio (4x filled cells). When a CSV or JSON dataset would exceed these limits, the original content is preserved in a safely fenced code block instead of being rendered as a table. Additionally, nested JSON values in table cells are now serialized in compact form (no indentation), and the JSON fallback path uses the same safe fencing helper, preventing both quadratic cell expansion and indentation-based output inflation.

cna.title: FlowIntel: Resource Exhaustion via Sparse CSV/JSON Table Expansion During File-to-Note Conversion

ai_annotations.description: Draft vulnerability metadata was generated from a git-format patch using an Ollama-hosted language model. Human validation is required before publication.

assumptions: PR:L assumes the file-to-note conversion feature requires an authenticated user with case access; the patch does not explicitly state authentication requirements, but FlowIntel is a case-management tool where case operations are typically authenticated.

VA:H assumes that exhausting a single worker has a meaningful availability impact on the service; if the deployment runs many redundant workers behind a load balancer, the practical impact could be lower.
CAPEC-124 is included as a secondary mapping; the primary mechanism is unbounded allocation (CAPEC-10), and the quadratic complexity is the underlying cause rather than a separate attack pattern.
The affected version range is taken from the explicit context (affected_version 0, fixed_version 4.1.0); the patch itself does not encode version boundaries.

The _fenced_content helper also mitigates a potential Markdown fence-injection issue (a crafted backtick sequence in the file content could break out of the code block), but the primary vulnerability addressed is resource exhaustion.

capecRationale.rationale: The attacker supplies a crafted CSV or JSON file that, when processed by the conversion feature, causes the application to allocate an excessive number of table cells, exhausting worker resources. This is a direct match to application resource exhaustion via crafted input.

The underlying mechanism is quadratic expansion: a file with N columns and M rows produces N*M padded cells. The attacker exploits the algorithmic complexity of the table-padding logic. This is a secondary, more specific mapping; CAPEC-10 is the primary match.

AC:L - crafting a sparse CSV/JSON file is straightforward; no race conditions or special timing required. AT:N - no prior tampering with system data needed. PR:L - requires an authenticated user with access to a case to attach and convert a file. UI:N - the conversion is triggered by the attacker's own action (uploading and converting the file); no victim interaction needed. VC:N, VI:N - no confidentiality or integrity impact. VA:H - worker exhaustion can deny service to other users of the FlowIntel instance. SC:N, SI:N, SA:N - no secondary component impact is evidenced.

When a CSV or JSON dataset would exceed these limits, the original content is preserved in a safely fenced code block instead of being rendered as a table. Additionally, nested JSON values in table cells are now serialized in compact form (no indentation), and the JSON fallback path uses the same safe fencing helper, preventing both quadratic cell expansion and indentation-based output inflation.

x_patch2vuln.patchSummary: In app/utils/file_converter.py: added constants MAX_PADDED_TABLE_CELLS (50000) and MAX_PADDING_RATIO (4); added helper _table_too_sparse() to detect oversized sparse tables; added helper _fenced_content() that generates a code fence long enough to prevent fence-injection from user content; modified convert_csv_to_note() to short-circuit to fenced output when the table is too sparse; modified convert_json_to_note() to apply the same sparse check for arrays of objects; changed json.dumps(value, indent=2) to json.dumps(value) for nested values in table cells; replaced the JSON fallback json.dumps(data, indent=2) with _fenced_content(content, "json"). ai_annotations.description: Draft vulnerability metadata was generated from a git-format patch using an Ollama-hosted language model. Human validation is required before publication.

patches.subject: fix: [security] Neutralise formulas in case and task CSV

x_patch2vuln.subject: fix: [security] Neutralise formulas in case and task CSV
x_patch2vuln.fixSummary: A shared CSV cell formatter (csv_safe_cell) is introduced that detects formula-like strings—those beginning with =, +, -, @, their fullwidth Unicode variants, or leading control/whitespace characters—and prefixes them with an apostrophe so spreadsheet applications treat the content as literal text. All case and task CSV export rows now pass every cell value through this formatter before writing, while numeric and ordinary text values are left unchanged.
assumptions: The affected version range is not explicitly stated in the patch; the metadata field 'affected_version' contains the placeholder value '0'. All versions prior to commit adef89f5 are assumed affected.

PR:L assumes the attacker needs at least editor-level access to create or modify case/task fields, based on the editor_required decorator visible in the surrounding code. If the application allows unauthenticated case creation, PR would be N.
The CVSS secondary-scope impact (SC:L, SI:L) assumes the victim's spreadsheet application executes injected formulas; actual impact depends on the specific application and its security settings.
CAPEC-117 (CSV Injection) is selected as the closest match; if this CAPEC ID is not present in the target CAPEC version, CAPEC-66 (Leverage Executable Code) would be the next-best alternative.

The fullwidth Unicode formula triggers (＝, ＋, －, ＠) are included in the fix, suggesting the developers considered non-ASCII bypass vectors; the CVSS does not separately account for this as it does not change the base score.
x_patch2vuln.patchSummary: New file app/utils/csv_utils.py defines csv_safe_cell(value) which returns an empty string for None, prepends an apostrophe to strings that start with tab/CR/LF or whose lstrip()-ed form begins with =, +, -, @, or fullwidth equivalents (＝, ＋, －, ＠), and otherwise returns the value unchanged. In app/tools/tools.py the _cases_to_csv function is modified so that both case rows and task rows are wrapped with a dict comprehension applying csv_safe_cell to every field before writer.writerow. The user manual (doc/user-manual.md) gains a note explaining the apostrophe-prefixing behaviour and that JSON exports preserve original text.
x_patch2vuln.cvssRationale: AV:N – exploitation occurs over the network via the web interface. AC:L – crafting formula-like text requires no special conditions. AT:N – no specific attack prerequisites. PR:L – the attacker needs editor-level access to create or modify case/task fields. UI:A – the victim must actively open the CSV in a spreadsheet application for the formula to execute. VC/VI/VA:N – the primary system (flowintel) suffers no direct confidentiality, integrity, or availability impact. SC:L – the secondary system (spreadsheet) may leak data via formula functions. SI:L – the secondary system's data integrity can be altered by injected formulas. SA:N – no availability impact on the secondary system.

capecRationale.rationale: The patch neutralises spreadsheet formula injection via CSV export, which is the canonical CSV Injection attack pattern. An attacker stores formula-like text in application fields; when the CSV is opened in a spreadsheet, the formula executes. CAPEC-117 is the most specific and directly applicable pattern. Confidence is high because the commit message, code changes, and documentation all explicitly reference spreadsheet formula neutralisation in CSV output.

weaknessRationale.rationale: The patch directly addresses the case where user-controlled text is written into a CSV file without neutralising spreadsheet formula triggers (=, +, -, @, fullwidth variants, control characters). This is the exact definition of CWE-147.
More broadly, the CSV output encoding did not escape or neutralise special characters that carry meaning in the downstream consumer (spreadsheet application), fitting the general CWE-116 category.

flowintel allows users with editor-level access to author case and task fields, including aggregated tags. When these records are exported as CSV, the field values are written verbatim into the output file.

Because no sanitisation is applied to user-supplied text before CSV serialisation, an attacker can store values that begin with spreadsheet formula triggers (such as =, +, -, @, or their fullwidth Unicode equivalents, or leading control/whitespace characters). When a victim opens the exported CSV in a spreadsheet application (e.g. Microsoft Excel, LibreOffice Calc), the stored text is interpreted and executed as a live formula rather than displayed as literal text.

This can lead to unintended data manipulation within the spreadsheet, potential data exfiltration via formula functions, or execution of downstream commands depending on the spreadsheet application and its configuration.

The vulnerability requires the victim to actively open the CSV file in a spreadsheet application; the flowintel application itself is not directly compromised.

Affected: <4.1.0

descriptions.description: CWE-147 Improper Neutralization of Input with Special Element Used for a Spreadsheet (CSV and DSL)

descriptions.value:
flowintel contains multiple authorization bypass vulnerabilities in its Analyzer (MISP Modules) functionality, affecting both the web interface and the REST API.

- Saving analyzer results to a case or task accepted caller-supplied case and task identifiers without verifying that the authenticated user is a member of the target case or holds the required restricted-task permissions. An authenticated user could write notes, create tasks, and attach MISP objects or attributes into another organization's case.

- Stored analyzer results were retrievable by UUID by any authenticated user. Both the web endpoint and the API endpoint returned the full result payload without checking ownership, exposing another user's analysis output.

- The save handler did not validate the structure of the request, did not reject conflicting destination selections, and did not halt processing when a task-note operation failed, allowing partial or unintended writes.

Preconditions: the attacker must possess a valid authenticated session (or API token) in flowintel. No administrative role is required.

Security impact: unauthorized cross-tenant data disclosure (analyzer results) and unauthorized cross-tenant data modification (notes, tasks, MISP objects/attributes in another organization's case).

Affected versions: flowintel prior to 4.1.0.
CAPEC-129 Parameter Tampering

descriptions.description: CWE-639 Authorization Bypass Through User-Controlled Key

solutions.value: The patch enforces authorization on both read and write paths for analyzer results. A new ownership/admin check gates result retrieval in both the web view and the API. Before any write operation, the target case is resolved and the caller's membership (or admin role) is verified; restricted-task permissions are additionally enforced. Input validation rejects malformed or conflicting destination selections, and task-note errors now abort the save. The front-end template was updated to surface 403 permission errors instead of silently treating them as generic failures.

descriptions.value:
Flowintel , contained a session management vulnerability in its browser authentication mechanism. The session identifier used a bare numeric user ID rather than a credential-bound token, resulting in several related weaknesses:

- Remembered logins (remember-me cookies) remained valid after a user changed their password, allowing an attacker holding a previously issued cookie to retain access indefinitely.
- Server-side session identifiers were not rotated upon login (local, SSO, or remembered), enabling session fixation.
- Self-service email and password changes did not require verification of the current password, permitting an attacker with an active session to modify account credentials without knowledge of the existing password.
- Administrator-initiated password resets did not revoke other browser sessions, invalidate remembered logins, or rotate the affected user's API key.

An attacker who obtained a valid session or remember-me cookie (e.g., through XSS, network interception, or cookie theft) could maintain unauthorized access even after the legitimate user changed their password. Additionally, an attacker with any valid session could change the account's email address or password without knowing the current credentials, effectively taking over the account.

Affected versions: Flowintel prior to 4.1.0.
CAPEC-18 Session Prediction
CAPEC-60 Session Hijacking

solutions.value: The fix binds browser session identifiers to the account's current credentials using an HMAC-SHA256 token derived from the user ID, auth provider, creation date, and password hash. All login paths (local, SSO, remembered) now rotate the server-side session ID. Self-service email and password changes require the current password. A self-service password change refreshes the owner's session while revoking all other browser sessions and remembered logins. Administrator password resets additionally rotate the user's API key. Legacy bare-ID session identifiers are rejected by the user loader, and session housekeeping code is updated to parse the new format safely.

assumptions: The affected version range is inferred from the explicit context (affected_version '0', fixed_version '4.1.0'); the patch itself does not enumerate specific prior versions.

CVSS PR:L assumes the attacker already holds a valid session or remember-me cookie; if the attacker must first obtain one via a separate vulnerability, the effective privilege requirement may be higher.
CVSS VC:L is assigned because a persistent session grants data access, but the primary impact is integrity (account takeover) rather than direct data exfiltration.

CAPEC-18 (Session Prediction) is selected as the closest match because the bare user ID is the root cause of the predictability; however, the patch's primary remediation is credential binding and session rotation rather than increasing token entropy, so the mapping is approximate.
The patch does not specify whether the vulnerability was reported through a coordinated disclosure process or a public channel; elhoim is credited as reporter based solely on the commit message.
The SSVC 'automatable: yes' assessment assumes the attacker can script session reuse or credential modification via HTTP requests; no evidence of an existing automated exploit is present.

capecRationale.rationale: The session identifier was a bare sequential user ID, making it trivially predictable. An attacker who knew or guessed a user's ID could construct a valid session identifier without any cryptographic secret. This is the closest CAPEC to the root cause: the session token lacked unpredictability and was not bound to any secret. The uncertainty is that the patch's primary fix is credential binding and session rotation rather than increasing token entropy, but the predictability of the bare ID is the enabling condition for the session persistence and fixation issues.

An attacker who obtained a valid session or remember-me cookie (via XSS, network sniffing, or other means) could maintain access after the legitimate user changed their password, effectively hijacking the session indefinitely. The lack of session revocation on credential change and the absence of session ID rotation made this hijack persistent. This is a secondary mapping; CAPEC-18 is preferred as the root cause, but CAPEC-60 better describes the attacker's end-to-end goal.

AT:N: No manipulation of the attack target is required. PR:L: The attacker needs a low-privilege valid session (any authenticated user) or a stolen remember-me cookie; no administrative access is required. UI:N: The session persists without any further user interaction; the victim does not need to perform any action for the attacker to retain access. VI:H: The attacker can change the account's email and password without knowing the current password, resulting in full account takeover and persistent unauthorized access. VA:H: The legitimate user's access is undermined by the attacker's persistent session, and the attacker can maintain indefinite access. SC/SI/SA:N: The impact is confined to the Flowintel application itself; no other components are directly affected.

weaknessRationale.rationale: The primary weakness is that browser sessions and remembered logins were not invalidated when credentials changed. The session identifier (a bare user ID) did not incorporate any credential state, so sessions outlived password changes and could be restored after deletion. This is a textbook insufficient session expiration issue.

Server-side session IDs were not rotated upon any login event (local, SSO, or remembered). An attacker could fix a known session ID before the victim authenticated and retain access afterward. The patch adds session ID regeneration on all authentication transitions.

The session identifier was a bare, predictable numeric user ID with no cryptographic binding to the account's credentials. This allowed session identifiers to be trivially guessed or forged by anyone who knew a user's ID, constituting improper authentication. The uncertainty is that the primary impact is session persistence rather than direct forgery, but the root cause is the lack of credential binding in the authentication token.

cna.title: Org.keycloak:keycloak-services: post-logout redirect uri configuration of a disabled client is still honored, leading to open redirect

descriptions.value: A flaw was found in Keycloak. The OpenID Connect (OIDC) logout endpoint continues to honor post-logout redirect rules for disabled clients rather than rejecting the requests. If a disabled client retains permissive redirect configurations, a remote attacker can exploit this issue by supplying an arbitrary redirection target in a logout request, leading to an open redirect that can be used in phishing attacks.

cna.x_redhatCweChain: CWE-601: URL Redirection to Untrusted Site

workarounds.value:
Administrators can mitigate this flaw by removing permissive redirect configurations from inactive clients or deleting unused clients:

1. In the Keycloak Admin Console, navigate to the relevant realm and inspect the 'Clients' list.
2. For any client set to disabled, open its settings and clear or restrict the 'Valid Post Logout Redirect URIs' and 'Valid Redirect URIs' fields, ensuring wildcard characters ('*') are removed and only explicitly trusted absolute URLs remain.
3. Alternatively, permanently delete any disabled clients that are obsolete and no longer required.

Caveats: Deleting a client permanently removes its configuration, mappers, service account roles, and credentials. Changes made to client settings in the Admin Console apply immediately to the realm without requiring a Keycloak service restart.

flowintel contains an information disclosure vulnerability in its case history feature. When a user views the history of a case they are authorized to access, the history output includes references to other cases (linked, unlinked, or forked) without verifying whether the requesting user has permission to view those referenced cases. This exposes the identifiers and titles of cases that the user should not be able to discover.

The vulnerability affects multiple output paths:
- Browser-based case history view
- API history endpoint
- Plain-text history download
- Markdown history download
- Report timeline generation

An authenticated user with access to any single case can enumerate the existence and identifiers of other cases by reading the history of a case they can access. This bypasses the intended per-case access control model and may reveal the existence of sensitive investigations, their identifiers, and associated metadata to unauthorized users.

The raw audit storage is not modified; the issue is solely in the presentation layer failing to filter references to inaccessible cases before returning history data to the user.

Affected versions: flowintel prior to 4.1.0.
CAPEC-128 Application Metadata Discovery

descriptions.description: CWE-200 Exposure of Sensitive Information to an Unauthorized Actor

solutions.value: A new visibility-aware history retrieval function was introduced that parses each history record for case references (link, unlink, fork events) and checks the requesting user's access to every referenced case before including that record in the output. Records referencing inaccessible cases are omitted from the response. The filtering is applied consistently across all history output paths (browser view, API, text download, Markdown download, and report timelines). Administrative users retain full unfiltered access. The raw audit log storage remains unchanged to preserve forensic integrity.

descriptions.value:
FlowIntel contained a Cross-Site Request Forgery (CSRF) vulnerability affecting fourteen web routes that performed destructive or state-changing operations. The affected routes accepted HTTP GET requests in addition to (or instead of) POST, which bypassed the Flask-WTF CSRF token validation that is only enforced on non-GET requests.

The vulnerable operations included:
- Case deletion and case merging
- Organisation removal from a case
- Task deletion (case and template)
- Case template and note template deletion
- Connector, connector instance, and icon deletion
- Custom tag deletion and status change
- Taxonomy and galaxy status changes

An attacker who could induce an authenticated user to follow a crafted link or load a page containing a cross-site navigation (e.g., an image tag or redirect) could trigger any of these destructive actions using the victim's session cookie, without the victim's explicit consent or awareness. No special privileges beyond a valid authenticated session with the appropriate role (editor or admin) were required on the victim's account.

Security impact: unauthorized deletion or modification of cases, tasks, templates, connectors, icons, custom tags, taxonomies, and galaxies belonging to the victim or the organisation, resulting in loss of data integrity.

Affected versions: FlowIntel prior to 4.1.0
CAPEC-124 Cross-Site Request Forgery

solutions.value: The vulnerability is remediated by restricting all fourteen affected web routes to accept only POST requests, ensuring that Flask-WTF's CSRF token validation is enforced. All fifteen client-side callers (JavaScript fetch calls and HTML template scripts) were updated to send POST requests with the page's CSRF token in the X-CSRFToken header, preserving legitimate user interactions while blocking cross-site forged requests.

descriptions.value:
Flowintel disabled TLS certificate verification for all MISP API connections and used unverified SSL contexts for IMAP and SMTP STARTTLS mail connections. This allowed an on-path (man-in-the-middle) attacker positioned between Flowintel and its MISP or mail servers to impersonate the remote server and intercept sensitive data.

Affected connections include:
- All MISP HTTPS API calls (event retrieval, attribute search, event creation, connectivity checks, and API validation)
- SMTP STARTTLS connections used for sending email notifications
- IMAP TLS connections used for fetching mail archives and testing connectivity

An attacker who can observe or intercept network traffic between Flowintel and the MISP or mail server could:
- Capture MISP API keys and mail credentials (SMTP/IMAP passwords)
- Read all threat intelligence data exchanged (events, attributes, objects, reports)
- Inject or modify threat intelligence data returned to Flowintel

The vulnerability required no authentication on the part of the attacker and no user interaction; it was exploitable by any party with a network position between Flowintel and its configured MISP or mail endpoints.

Affected versions: Flowintel prior to 4.1.0.
CAPEC-119 Man-in-the-Middle

solutions.value: The fix introduces a shared TLS utility module that enforces certificate and hostname verification by default for all MISP and mail connections. MISP clients now receive a proper SSL verification context instead of ssl=False, and IMAP/SMTP connections use a verified ssl.SSLContext. Operators may configure a private CA bundle path or explicitly disable verification (which fails closed on malformed input). The previous urllib3 warning suppression is removed, and upgrade documentation warns that previously accepted self-signed or mismatched certificates will now cause connection failures.

cna.title: Flowintel Disables TLS Certificate Verification for MISP and Mail Connections

CAPEC-119 (Man-in-the-Middle) is selected as the closest standard attack pattern; the patch does not reference a specific CAPEC, and the attack could also be described under CAPEC-123 (Session Hijacking) or CAPEC-107 (Web Service Cross-Site Request Forgery) in a broader sense, but CAPEC-119 most directly matches the described on-path interception scenario.
The patch assumes MISP connector URLs use HTTPS; if an operator configures a plain HTTP MISP URL, TLS verification is not applicable and the vulnerability does not manifest in the same way.

The patch commit message explicitly references an 'on-path attacker' impersonating the server, confirming this mapping.

Flowintel's template repository subsystem did not adequately constrain file access to the configured repository base directory. Two related weaknesses existed:

- Repository registration and editing accepted arbitrary local paths without verifying they resolved inside the configured REPOSITORY_BASE_PATH, allowing an authenticated user to point a repository at any readable directory on the host.
- Manifest and template file lookups used normalized (non-canonical) path joins and a startswith-based guard that could be bypassed by symbolic links, permitting reads of files outside the intended repository.

An authenticated user with the ability to add or edit a template repository could therefore cause the application to read and return the contents of arbitrary files readable by the service account, including configuration files, credentials, or other sensitive data.

Affected: Flowintel versions prior to 4.1.0.
CAPEC-126 Path Traversal

descriptions.description: CWE-22 Improper Limitation of a Pathname to a Restricted Directory ('Path Traversal')
CWE-59 Improper Link Resolution Before File Access ('Link Following')

solutions.value: The fix introduces canonical (realpath-based) path resolution and enforces that every repository root and every child file or directory resolves within the configured REPOSITORY_BASE_PATH using os.path.commonpath. All code paths that previously performed raw os.path.join or normpath operations (registration, editing, discovery scan, entry scan, manifest read, and template file read) now go through the new validated helpers. Scans that encounter an escaping path roll back any partial database updates and return an error, preventing partial state corruption.

descriptions.value:
FlowIntel contains a missing authorization vulnerability in its task file deletion functionality. When a privileged task is in a restricted state (Requested, Rejected, or Request Review), any authenticated user with basic case membership (e.g., editor or queuer) was able to delete evidence files associated with that task via both the browser interface and the REST API. The deletion operation should have been restricted to users holding Admin, Case Admin, or Queue Admin roles.

The vulnerability affects the core file deletion logic, the browser-facing task endpoint, and the API task endpoint. No role-based restriction was enforced prior to performing disk removal, database record deletion, timeline event removal, or history log updates.

An attacker with a low-privilege case membership could destroy evidence files, corrupt investigation timelines, and alter case history, compromising the integrity of ongoing investigations.

Affected versions: FlowIntel prior to 4.1.0.
CAPEC-126 Forced Browsing

solutions.value: The fix enforces role-based authorization before any file deletion side effects occur. It verifies that the file belongs to the specified task (preventing task substitution) and that, when the task is in a restricted state, the requesting user holds Admin, Case Admin, or Queue Admin privileges. Denial is returned with a 403 status and an audit log entry before any disk, database, timeline, or history modification takes place. The check is applied consistently across the core model, the browser endpoint, and the API endpoint.

cna.title: FlowIntel Missing Authorization Check Allows Unauthorized Deletion of Evidence Files from Restricted Privileged Tasks

ai_annotations.description: Draft vulnerability metadata was generated from a git-format patch using an Ollama-hosted language model. Human validation is required before publication.

assumptions: The affected version range is inferred from the explicit context (affected_version 0, fixed_version 4.1.0); no intermediate version boundaries are confirmed.
CAPEC-126 is selected as the closest available attack pattern; a more specific CAPEC for missing role-based authorization on a known endpoint does not exist in the catalog.

CVSS VI is rated High based on the permanent destruction of evidence files and alteration of investigation records; if the deployment context limits the scope of affected tasks, the impact could be lower.

The patch references a 'can_edit_requested_task' permission and 'is_task_restricted' state check; the exact role hierarchy and whether Queue Admin is a distinct role from Case Admin is assumed from the commit message and test fixtures.
No evidence of active exploitation or public disclosure is present in the patch; SSVC exploitation is set to none.

capecRationale.rationale: The attacker accesses a resource (file deletion endpoint) that they are not authorized to invoke based on their role. While CAPEC-126 typically describes URL guessing, the underlying pattern is the same: the application fails to enforce authorization on a known endpoint, allowing an authenticated but low-privilege user to perform an operation they should not. This is the closest CAPEC to a missing role-based authorization check on a known API/browser endpoint. Uncertainty: a more precise CAPEC for 'missing authorization on a known endpoint' does not exist in the CAPEC catalog, so CAPEC-126 is the best available match.

PR:L: The attacker needs a low-privilege authenticated account with case membership (editor or queuer). UI:N: No victim interaction is required. VC:N: No confidential data is exposed. descriptions.value:
FlowIntel contains an authorization bypass in its task management workflow. When a user reopens a completed task (by toggling its completion state or changing its status to a non-finished value) or creates a new task within a completed privileged case, the parent case is automatically revived (un-completed, status reset to Created, finish date cleared). The system failed to enforce the required Admin or Case Admin privilege check before performing this case revival side effect.

A user with basic task-level permissions (e.g., editor, queuer, or queue admin) could trigger the revival of a completed privileged case through the browser interface or the REST API, without holding the elevated role required for case-level operations. This could disrupt case lifecycle management, clear completion metadata, and potentially expose the case to further unauthorized modifications.

The vulnerability affects both the browser-based task completion/status-change endpoints and the corresponding API endpoints, as well as the task creation flow.

Affected versions: FlowIntel prior to 4.1.0.
CAPEC-114 Forced Browsing

solutions.value: The fix introduces explicit authorization checks (can_reopen_case and can_reopen_task) that require Admin or Case Admin privileges before a completed privileged case can be revived as a side effect of task reopening or task creation. Denial is enforced at the core model layer and at both the browser and API endpoint layers, with audit logging of denied attempts. Legitimate task creation is preserved, but the automatic case revival is suppressed for unauthorized users.

A vulnerability exists in the flowintel application's calendar functionality that allows unauthorized access to private case data. The task calendar queries failed to enforce visibility checks on the parent case associated with tasks. Specifically, tasks assigned to a user or belonging to the user's organization were returned in calendar views (including browser and API ICS feeds) without verifying whether the user had permission to view the parent case. This allowed users to potentially discover and access details of private cases they were not authorized to view, leading to information disclosure.

The issue affected the default task visibility logic and the assigned-only task queries. The fix ensures that case visibility is rechecked in addition to task assignment or organization membership, preventing the exposure of private case data in calendar outputs.

Affected versions: flowintel < 4.1.0
CAPEC-126 Forced Browsing

descriptions.description: CWE-639 Authorization Bypass Through User-Controlled Key

solutions.value: The vulnerability is remediated by adding explicit case visibility checks to the task calendar queries. The fix ensures that tasks are only visible if the user has permission to view the parent case, in addition to being assigned to the task or belonging to the same organization. This prevents the disclosure of private case data in calendar views and ICS feeds.

descriptions.value: A flaw was found in Keycloak. This vulnerability allows an authenticated remote attacker to cause a denial of service by terminating active sessions of arbitrary users. Flowintel contains multiple SSO identity and organisation trust boundary violations that collectively allow account takeover, privilege escalation, and unauthorized access to private case data.

- Keycloak SSO accepted unverified email claims, and all SSO providers (Keycloak, Entra ID, SimpleSAML) could resolve a claimed email address to an existing account that was created via a different sign-in method, enabling cross-provider account collision and unauthorized access to another user's account and data.

- Entra ID role mapping relied on group display names, which tenant members could duplicate by creating a group with the same name as a privileged group (e.g. FlowintelAdmin), resulting in unauthorized role escalation.

- SSO provisioning reused organisations whose display names matched user-controlled profile names, granting the new SSO user access to that organisation's private cases without explicit administrator assignment.

- Case sharing via the API resolved organisations by name using a first-match query, so ambiguous names could silently resolve to the wrong organisation.

Preconditions: an attacker must have a valid SSO identity (Keycloak, Entra ID, or SimpleSAML) or be a member of the relevant Entra tenant. No local administrator access is required.

Security impact: unauthorized access to private case data, privilege escalation to Editor or higher roles, and account takeover across authentication providers.

Affected versions: Flowintel prior to 4.1.0.
CAPEC-126 Exploiting Incorrectly Handled Edge Cases

descriptions.description: CWE-639 Authorization Bypass Through User-Controlled Key

solutions.value: The fix enforces strict identity and organisation trust boundaries across all SSO providers. Keycloak now requires a verified email claim and no longer falls back to preferred_username. A new shared identity-resolution function rejects any email that maps to an account registered under a different sign-in provider, preventing cross-provider account collision. Entra ID role mapping now requires configured group object IDs (UUIDs) instead of display names, eliminating the name-duplication escalation vector. Default organisation creation always allocates a new organisation rather than reusing one by name match. Case sharing via the API now rejects ambiguous organisation names and requires an explicit organisation ID.

FlowIntel, a threat intelligence case management platform, contains an information disclosure vulnerability in its case serialization logic. When a case is rendered via the REST API or browser views, all connector instances associated with that case were included in the response regardless of the requesting user's permissions.

This means that any authenticated user with read access to a case could observe connector metadata belonging to other users (personal-scope connectors) or other organizations (org-scope connectors), including connector URLs, descriptions, UUIDs, and potentially embedded API credentials.

Preconditions:
- An authenticated user account with at least read access to the affected case
- The case must have connector instances attached that belong to other users or organizations

Impact:
- Disclosure of personal connector endpoints and credentials of other users
- Disclosure of organization-scoped connector metadata across organizational boundaries
- Enumeration of connector infrastructure (URLs, UUIDs, descriptions) not intended for the viewer

Affected versions: < 4.1.0
CAPEC-1 Software Feature Discovery

descriptions.description: CWE-668 Exposure of Resource to Wrong Sphere

solutions.value: The fix introduces viewer-scoped authorization checks during case serialization. Connector instances are now filtered based on the acting user's permissions: administrators and assigned case-administrators retain full visibility, while regular users only see connectors whose sharing scope (personal, org, or global) grants them access. When no authenticated user context is available, connector metadata is omitted entirely. Credential-use checks for module execution remain unchanged.

MISP contains an authorization and input-validation flaw in its event push mechanism. When a user with push permissions initiates a push of events to a remote MISP instance, the system fails to enforce two critical checks: (1) it does not verify that an event is published before including it in the push, allowing unpublished (i.e., not yet publicly shared) events to be transmitted to the remote server; and (2) it does not verify that the pushing user has read access to the event, causing events the user cannot fetch to be sent as empty event shells, thereby disclosing the existence and metadata of events the user is not authorized to view. Additionally, the remote server's reply selecting which offered events to accept is used without validating that the selected identifiers actually correspond to events in the offered set, potentially allowing the remote to reference events outside the intended scope. The vulnerability requires an authenticated user with push permissions on the source MISP instance and a configured push target. The security impact is unauthorized disclosure of confidential threat-intelligence data (unpublished events and events restricted by user permissions) to a remote MISP instance that should not receive them.

assumptions: The affected MISP version range is not specified in the patch; all versions prior to this commit are assumed affected.
PR:L assumes the attacker needs a standard authenticated user with push permissions; if push is restricted to administrators only, PR could be H.

VC:L assumes the disclosed data (unpublished events, inaccessible event metadata) constitutes a low confidentiality impact; if the events contain highly sensitive threat intelligence, the impact could be higher.
CAPEC-126 is the closest available mapping; no CAPEC precisely describes 'missing authorization on outbound data push in a trusted inter-system exchange.'

The remote server's ability to reference non-offered events (CWE-20 component) is assessed as low impact because the events would still need to exist and be accessible on the source; the primary impact is the authorization bypass (CWE-862).
The 'Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5' credit is included as listed in the commit metadata; its role as a remediation developer is inferred from the co-authorship line.
x_patch2vuln.fixSummary: The fix enforces three security controls in the push path: (1) an explicit check that the event's 'published' flag is set before the event is eligible for push, returning a descriptive error if it is not; (2) a guard that skips any event for which the pushing user's fetch returns empty, preventing transmission of inaccessible events as empty shells; and (3) validation of the remote server's event-selection reply so that only UUIDs present in the originally offered event list are accepted, discarding any identifiers the remote references that were not part of the push offer.
x_patch2vuln.patchSummary: In app/Model/Event.php, a new early-return check is added at the top of uploadEventToServer() that rejects the push if $event['Event']['published'] is empty. In app/Model/Server.php, three changes are made: (a) in the push() loop, a 'continue' statement is added when fetchEvent() returns empty, skipping inaccessible events; (b) the lastpushedid fallback logic is corrected to preserve the existing value when both successes and fails are empty; (c) in getEventIdsForPush(), the remote's JSON reply is validated as an array, filtered to string values, and then cross-referenced against the UUIDs in the $request (offered events) array so that only UUIDs present in both sets are returned.
x_patch2vuln.cvssRationale: AV:N: The push occurs over the network between MISP instances. AC:L: Triggering a push is a standard user action with no special race or timing conditions. AT:N: No manipulation of the attack target is required. PR:L: An authenticated user with push permissions is required. UI:N: No additional user interaction beyond initiating the push. VC:L: Confidential event data (unpublished events, events the user cannot access) is disclosed to the remote server. VI:N, VA:N: No integrity or availability impact on the source. SC:N, SI:N, SA:N: The remote server receives data but its own confidentiality, integrity, and availability are not compromised.

weaknessRationale.rationale: The push mechanism does not enforce that events are published or that the pushing user has read access before transmitting them to a remote server, constituting a missing authorization check on data egress.

The remote server's reply selecting events to accept is used without validating that the referenced identifiers belong to the set of events actually offered in the push request, allowing out-of-scope references.

capecRationale.rationale: The MISP push mechanism relies on a trusted relationship between the source and remote MISP instances. The source trusts the push flow and the remote's reply without enforcing proper authorization (published status, user access) or validating the remote's selection against the offered set. The closest CAPEC is Leverage Trusted Relationship because the vulnerability arises from insufficient validation within a trusted inter-system data exchange. Uncertainty: no CAPEC perfectly captures 'missing authorization on outbound data push'; CAPEC-126 is the best available match for a trusted-relationship data-flow flaw.

descriptions.value:
FlowIntel contains an authorization flaw in its duplicate alert ingestion logic. When a duplicate alert is received and its content is updated, the ownership and visibility scope fields (owner user and owner organization) were not refreshed to reflect the connector's current scope. As a result, an alert that was originally created under a broader visibility scope retained that broader scope even after the connector's scope was narrowed or changed.

This means that users or organizations that should no longer have visibility into a given alert could continue to access it, because the stale ownership fields were never updated during the duplicate-update path. The issue affected all duplicate updates, including those involving alerts in terminal review states and those recovered from uniqueness conflicts.

Security impact:
- Unauthorized disclosure of security alert content to users or organizations outside the intended visibility scope.
- Stale access persists indefinitely until the alert is independently re-scoped or deleted.

Affected version: <4.1.0.
